title: The realitly of small accounts... with small targets, fees turn it into a loser (simple math)
author: LuckOrEdge
selftext:
I know this is fairly basic and a rookie mistake, but I wasted the last week building and testing a model I thought had a real edge in the market. Only to realize I forgot to account for fees and the edge disapeared. 

One of the unfortunate truth in trading is that begginer traders that often use small accounts, will have fees usually completely destroy any edge they have. 

Take a bot that wins 55% of its trades, with its stop the same size as its target (1:1 risk to reward). Let's account for fees plus slippage cost $10 a round trip.

That $10 is the same on every trade. Only the target changes:

* **$20 target:** a win nets $10, a loss costs $30. It needs 75% winners. At 55%, it loses $8 a trade.
* **$50 target:** needs 60%. Loses $5 a trade.
* **$100 target:** needs 55%. Breaks even.
* **$200 target:** needs 52.5%. Makes $10 a trade.

Before fees, this bot makes money at every target size. After fees, the small targets lose.

Always account for fees and slippage on any backtest, especially small accounts.

What does your bot pay per trade?

comments.author: Awkward_Lie_6635
comments.body: It would take special effort for an AI not to mention fees play a part.

replies.author: LuckOrEdge
replies.body: That is true and that is exactly what happened. I usually backtest my strategy in anothet platform and cross validate the results using AI.

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
This is one of the most under-appreciated killers of retail edges.

I’ve gone through a lot of papers and old threads looking for something that survives contact with reality, and fees + slippage are where a lot of “edges” quietly die. Especially once you move from backtest land to actual small account sizes.

The 55% win rate example is solid. Before costs it looks fine, after costs the small targets are pure dead weight. A lot of people (myself included at some point) only figure this out after spending time building something that looked good on paper.

Curious what others here are actually paying per round trip on their live bots. If anyone’s working on setups where the edge is wide enough that $5–10 of friction doesn’t just erase it — open to bouncing ideas or teaming up on something instead of just repeating the cycle alone.

replies.author: LuckOrEdge
replies.body: You can usually get comfortably around 0.50$ a trade. If you account for APIs and other fees, it's easily 1$ a trade. On prop firms account it's around 1-2$ a trade.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good lesson, and posting it will save others the same week of work. Fees hit small targets so hard because they're a fixed cost on every trade, so the break-even win rate climbs fast as the target shrinks. I'd add slippage as its own line, since it often grows when you trade more often or in thin markets. A quick check is to rerun the backtest with the fee doubled, and if the edge disappears, it was never strong enough. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting, so fees are part of the test from the start.

replies.author: LuckOrEdge
replies.body: That's true slippage varies widely from instrument to instrument.
